# Synthesis Principles {.unnumbered}

Part VII synthesizes the six operational subsystems into an enduring architecture for autonomous machine learning systems. Moving beyond the boundaries of digital execution sandboxes, we establish the timeless systems invariants that survive foundation model weight turnover, analyze the physical limits of compounding trajectory scaling, and confront the cyber-physical frontier where digital software agents meet the irreversible constraints of embodied robotic systems.

::: {#pri-vol3-invariant-closure .callout-principle title="Invariant closure at trajectory boundaries"}

**Invariant**: System safety, capability bounds, and resource allocations cannot be guaranteed per-token or per-inference; they must achieve formal closure across the complete multi-step trajectory runtime.

**Implication**: Outer supervisors and kernel isolation layers must enforce hard operational boundaries, taint propagation, and spend quotas external to the stochastic model weights.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-reversibility-boundary .callout-principle title="The physical reversibility boundary"}

**Invariant**: In digital software systems, speculative execution errors can be rolled back via copy-on-write snapshots; in embodied physical environments, Newtonian mechanics and entropy render actuation strictly irreversible.

**Implication**: Physical AI systems require hard real-time safety envelopes, provably safe fallback controllers, and dual-rate control loops that decouple slow neural deliberation from high-frequency actuation.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry .callout-principle title="The verification asymmetry principle"}

**Invariant**: Evaluating whether a multi-step trajectory satisfied an objective is computationally and sample-efficiently cheaper than generating the valid trajectory from scratch ($C_{\text{verify}} \ll C_{\text{generate}}$).

**Implication**: Scalable autonomous systems must leverage deterministic verification oracles and process reward models to guide test-time deliberation, trajectory filtering, and policy optimization.

:::
